structured_output.summary: The hypothesis tree is empty, so this is the starting evidence. The closest prior result is a CIFAR-100 entry for this exact benchmark (Daniel-T-S-Adams/CIFAR-100-speedrun), submitted today (2026-10-03) at a hackathon. It adapts Keller Jordan's airbench96 network and reports 75.29% accuracy in 8.11 s on an A100-SXM4-80GB. The benchmark's own baseline is 75.36% in 59.30 s. The 75.29% would fall short of our 0.753 bar, and the source alternately reports 75.5%. The PR page now returns 404, so I only saw its settings through search snippets: 3 convolutions per group, widths 128/384/576, label smoothing 0.3 (better than 0.2 and 0.4), lr 9.0, weight decay 0.012, 8.5 epochs, picked from about 40 configurations. I could not confirm whether it used test-time augmentation (TTA), which RULES.md forbids. Airbench's published speed depends partly on TTA, worth about 0.65 percentage points (roughly 1.2 epochs saved). Without it, a rule-compliant airbench recipe will likely need more epochs or a wider network. Levers that cut wall-clock time on CIFAR-10 at the same accuracy: the Muon optimizer with batch size 2000 and 8 epochs (3.09 s to 2.59 s); hard-example selection with a small proxy model (34.7 s to 27.3 s at 96%); and Hiverge's engineering changes (vectorized optimizer, compiled training step, SiLU instead of GELU, parallel augmentation; 2.59 s to 1.99 s, though about one of those six changes is TTA, which we can't use). Suggested starting hypotheses: H1, airbench96-style network at about 8–10 epochs without TTA as the base; H2, Muon plus a larger batch to cut epochs; H3, proxy-model hard-example selection; H4, systems work (compile, channels_last, fp16/bf16, fused or vectorized optimizer); H5, label smoothing around 0.3 for CIFAR-100; H6, progressive or low-resolution training early on.

findings.source: https://github.com/abdullah-athar/iterate-futurebiohackers/pull/3 (PR title and search snippets; the page now returns 404)
findings.claim: An airbench96-based CIFAR-100 recipe on this exact benchmark reached 75.29% mean accuracy in 8.11 s mean prepare+train on a Modal A100-SXM4-80GB; the organizer baseline is 75.36% in 59.30 s. Settings: 3 convolutions per group, widths 128/384/576 (widening the last block from 512 to 576 'adds accuracy with little additional compute'), label smoothing 0.3, lr 9.0, wd 0.012, 8.5 epochs, chosen from about 40 swept configurations. torch.compile and warmup on synthetic data run in build(); GPU transfer, normalization and whitening init run in prepare().
findings.relevance: Gives a strong starting recipe and a time to beat (about 8 s). But 75.29% is below our 0.753 bar, so this exact recipe probably needs slightly more epochs or width. It is also unclear whether it used TTA, which RULES.md forbids; if it did, a compliant version would lose more accuracy.
hypotheses: new: H1 airbench96-style net (128/384/~576, depth 3) at about 9–10 epochs without TTA reaches ≥75.3%
new: H1.x widening the last block is a cheap way to gain accuracy
new: H5 label smoothing 0.3 is better than 0.2 on CIFAR-100

findings.claim: Evaluation forbids 'additional augmented views (test-time augmentation), fitting, adaptation, test-set statistics'. Whitening and other preprocessing count toward timed prepare/train. Compiled code and allocated memory may be reused across trials, but learned values may not. Benchmark baseline is a ResNet9-style net, 40 epochs, width 64: 75.36% in 59.30 s on an A100 80GB PCIe.
findings.relevance: Rules out airbench's built-in TTA (level 2: mirror plus translate). Fitting the patch-whitening layer from data is allowed but timed. Compiling and warming up in build() is free.
hypotheses: new: H4 doing all compile and autotune work in build() removes it from the score

findings.claim: airbench94 ablations, in epochs saved to reach 94%: frozen patch-whitening about 13 epochs (more than doubles speed); identity (dirac) init 3 (21→18); scaling the BatchNorm bias learning rate 64x about 4.5 (18→13.5); lookahead about 1.5 (13.5→12); multi-crop TTA about 1.2 (12→10.8); alternating flip about 0.9 (10.8→9.9). TTA adds about 0.65 points (94.32→94.97 in one comparison). On CIFAR-100, airbench96 (45 epochs) reaches 79.27% (79.76% with Cutout) vs ResNet-18's 77.54%.
findings.relevance: Shows which airbench components matter most. Removing TTA, which we must, costs about 1.2 epochs-equivalent or about 0.6 points of accuracy. airbench96's 79% at 45 epochs leaves a lot of room to cut epochs toward 75%.
hypotheses: new: H1.x removing TTA costs about 0.5–0.7 points; make it up with about 1–1.5 extra epochs
new: H1.x keep whitening, dirac init, BatchNorm-bias lr scaling, lookahead and alternating flip

findings.claim: airbench94_muon: Muon(lr=0.24, momentum=0.6, nesterov) for 4D conv filters; SGD (momentum 0.85, nesterov, fused) for biases and head (lr 0.053 / 0.67); batch size 2000, 8 epochs, linear decay to zero; fp16 with BatchNorm in fp32, channels_last, compile mode max-autotune; 94.01% in 2.59 s vs 3.09 s for the compiled SGD airbench94 (9.9 epochs, batch size 1024). That is about 16% less time at the same accuracy.
findings.relevance: Muon with a larger batch is the strongest known change on CIFAR-10 for cutting epochs and time at equal accuracy. It has not been tested on CIFAR-100 at this scale.
hypotheses: new: H2 Muon on conv filters plus batch size about 2000 reaches 75.3% in fewer epochs and less time than SGD-Nesterov

findings.claim: airbench96_faster scores each batch of 1024 with a small proxy model and trains only on the hardest 512 by loss (mask[loss1.argsort()[-512:]]). Time to 96% falls from 34.7 s to 27.3 s (PFLOPs 4.9 to 3.1). Config: widths 128/384/512, depth 3, batch size 1024, lr 9.0, momentum 0.85, wd 0.012, label smoothing 0.2, cutout 12, translate 4, lookahead with a cubic alpha schedule.
findings.relevance: Proxy-model hard-example selection gave about a 21% speedup in a longer training regime. For a roughly 9-epoch run the proxy's overhead is a larger share, so the gain is unclear.
hypotheses: new: H3 training on the hardest half of each batch (chosen by a proxy model) reduces time to 75.3%

findings.claim: The CIFAR-10 94% record fell from 2.59 s to 1.99 s (more than 20%) on an A100. Changes: a vectorized Muon (batching parameter updates with padded matrices), a compiled training step, SiLU instead of GELU, a new whitening-filter init, parallelized crop augmentation plus brightness/contrast jitter, tuned lr/momentum/steps/memory format, and selective TTA (forbidden here). No per-change breakdown is given.
findings.relevance: At these few-second scales, engineering overhead (optimizer launches, augmentation, Python) makes up much of the time. Kernel- and system-level fixes on top of a good recipe are worth about 20%.
hypotheses: new: H4 systems work (vectorized/fused optimizer, compiled step, augmentation on the GPU, SiLU) cuts time by 10–20% at fixed accuracy

findings.claim: Progressive resizing (training on smaller images early, growing back to full size) improves wall-clock time with small accuracy cost on ImageNet ResNets. For CIFAR-10 ResNet-56, cropping works better than downscaling. The CPU or dataloader can become the bottleneck in early low-resolution epochs.
findings.relevance: An option the airbench line hasn't tried. Data stays on the GPU here, so the dataloader bottleneck is unlikely. But on 32x32 images the gain is uncertain and torch.compile would have to recompile for each new image size (doable in build()).
hypotheses: new: H6 training the early epochs at lower resolution (e.g. 24 px) cuts time at equal final accuracy

findings.claim: A 'critical damping' momentum schedule on CIFAR-100 reaches mid-training accuracy thresholds 2–4x sooner but costs 1.7 points at the end; at matched final accuracy the gain is only 1.14x.
findings.relevance: Weak evidence that momentum-schedule tricks matter less on CIFAR-100 than on CIFAR-10 once final accuracy is held fixed.
hypotheses: new: low priority, momentum-schedule tweaks are unlikely to beat retuning epochs or lr
